# ggplot3d

*three-dimensional plots with ggplot2*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/ggplot3d/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/ggplot3d/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/ggplot3d/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/ggplot3d)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

ggplot3d draws three-dimensional points, paths, surfaces and solids with [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/).

The package extends ggplot2's grammar of graphics with a z position scale and a camera. Each panel combines its layers into a scene, the collection of geometry used to determine which parts are visible. You can map variables to position, colour and fill, choose a view, and save the plot with `ggsave()`.

ggplot3d supports:

* Surfaces with observations, contours and fitted values.
* Columns, extruded polygons and indexed meshes.
* Continuous, discrete and date/time z scales, including transformations and facets.
* Vector drawing and raster rendering from the same scene geometry.

[Visibility](vignettes/visibility.Rmd) explains how overlapping geometry is ordered and split. The examples below generate their figures from the package.

## Installation

The development version compiles C++17 code. Install build tools for your operating system:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) matching your R version |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Install the development package:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/ggplot3d")
```

## Usage

1. Map three position columns with `aes()`.
2. Add a three-dimensional layer and `coord_3d()`.

The data below contain a regular grid of x and y positions and a height z. A surface connects neighbouring grid positions. The point layer marks selected positions above and below that surface.

```{r surface-points, fig.alt="A curved blue surface with red observations above and below it, partially hidden by the surface."}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)

surface <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 15),
                       y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 15))
surface$z <- with(surface, exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / 2))
observations <- surface[c(49, 73, 97, 121, 145, 169), ]
observations$z <- observations$z + c(0.3, -0.3, 0.3, -0.3, 0.3, -0.3)

ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "#2E6F9E") +
  geom_point_3d(data = observations, colour = "#B5342B", size = 3) +
  coord_3d()
```

The result is a ggplot object. Layer geometry is depth-sorted together within the panel, including where the surface covers a point.

## Intersecting surfaces

Each surface has its own data and fill. Their intersection determines which pieces are visible from the chosen camera.

```{r intersections, fig.alt="Blue and orange sloping surfaces intersect along their middle."}
first <- surface
first$z <- with(first, 0.6 * x)
second <- surface
second$z <- with(second, -0.6 * x + 0.2 * y)

ggplot(first, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "#2E6F9E") +
  geom_surface_3d(data = second, fill = "#9E5E0F") +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -45, elevation = 60)
```

## Columns

Map z to the top of each column. The default baseline is zero; `zmin` supplies a baseline from the data.

```{r columns, fig.alt="Nine blue columns on a three-by-three grid with different heights."}
columns <- expand.grid(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)
columns$z <- c(2, 4, 3, 5, 2, 4, 3, 6, 2)

ggplot(columns, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_col_3d(fill = "#2E6F9E", width = 0.65, depth = 0.65) +
  coord_3d()
```

## Raster output

A raster backend draws the scene into pixels at the requested resolution. It is useful for dense geometry and fixed-size images. Set it inside the coordinate system.

```{r raster, fig.alt="A raster rendering of the curved blue surface and red observations."}
raster_plot <- ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "#2E6F9E") +
  geom_point_3d(data = observations, colour = "#B5342B", size = 3) +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 144, antialias = 2))
raster_plot
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
ggsave("surface.png", raster_plot, width = 5, height = 4.5, dpi = 144)
```

## Documentation

Start with [Get started](vignettes/ggplot3d.Rmd) to create and save a plot.

* [The z scale](vignettes/z-scale.Rmd): transformations, categories, limits and facets.
* [Layers](vignettes/layers.Rmd): examples of every three-dimensional geom and stat.
* [Camera and framing](vignettes/camera.Rmd): view angles, projections and plot bounds.
* [Output backends](vignettes/backends.Rmd): choose vector or raster rendering.
* [Visibility](vignettes/visibility.Rmd): how the scene resolves overlapping geometry.

Function help is available in R, for example `?coord_3d` and `?geom_surface_3d`.

## Getting help

Send questions and bug reports to [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/ggplot3d/issues). Include a small reproducible example, the rendering backend, and `sessionInfo()`.
